title: Intro to Excel
objectives: By the end you can name any cell by its address and jump to it with the Name Box.
about: Excel keeps your information in a grid called a worksheet. Every box in the grid is a cell. Every cell has an address made of its column letter and its row number, such as C4. You use addresses whenever you read a formula, follow instructions, or tell a colleague where to look. To find an address, read the column letter across the top. Then read the row number down the side, and look where they meet. The cell with the thick green border is the active cell, and whatever you type goes into it. To reach a far-away cell, type its address in the Name Box, at the top left, and press Enter.
where_to_find: Name Box: the small box to the left of the formula bar. Click it, type an address such as D7, then press Enter.
Active cell: the cell with the thick green border. It receives whatever you type.

examples.scenario: A market stall owner wants to read Tuesday's takings.
examples.why: Column B holds takings and row 3 holds Tuesday, so B3 is where they meet.

examples.scenario: A teacher wants to point at all of Amina's scores.
examples.why: A range joins two corner cells with a colon. It means from B2 through D2.

examples.scenario: A clerk must reach cell F9 in a long invoice sheet.
examples.formula: Type F9 in the Name Box, then press Enter
examples.result: The active cell moves to F9
examples.why: The Name Box jumps there at once, however far away the cell is.

examples.scenario: A shop assistant records a new stock count for Paper.
examples.why: Typing replaces the contents of the active cell. Check the green border before you type.

watch_out: Write the column letter first: C4 is a cell, 4C is not.
Your typing goes into the active cell, the one with the thick green border. Check it before you type.
recap: You can now name any cell and any range and jump to them. Next, you will move between cells with Tab and Enter.

steps.prompt: You run a market stall. Wednesday's takings of 150 are missing from the table. Click the cell where column B meets Wednesday's row, type 150, and press Enter.
hints: Which row is Wednesday in? Which column holds the takings?
Takings are in column B and Wednesday is in row 4. The cell you want is where that column and that row meet. Click it, then type.
Click B4, type 150, and press Enter. B4 is column B (Takings) and row 4 (Wednesday). Enter saves the number in the cell.
steps.explanation: Column B holds takings and row 4 holds Wednesday, so the cell is B4. Typing puts the number in the active cell, and Enter saves it.

common_mistakes.message: B4 is still empty. Type 150 and press Enter to save it.
150 went into A4, the Day column. Takings are in column B.
B5 is Thursday's row. Wednesday is row 4.

steps.prompt: You manage invoices. Invoice INV-102 has been paid. Use the Name Box to jump to its Status cell, change it to Paid, and press Enter.
hints: Find INV-102's row first. Then find the Status column.
The Name Box is the small box left of the formula bar. Type an address there and press Enter to jump. INV-102 is in row 3 and Status is column D.
Type D3 in the Name Box and press Enter. The cursor jumps to D3. Now type Paid and press Enter to save it.
steps.explanation: INV-102 is in row 3 and Status is column D, so the cell is D3. The Name Box jumps straight there.

common_mistakes.message: That is INV-101's status. INV-102 is one row lower.
D3 still says Open. After jumping, type Paid and press Enter.
That is the Amount column. Status is column D.

steps.prompt: Your manager wants Gadget's three monthly figures formatted. Select just those figures, from January to March, in Gadget's row.
hints: A range has two corners. Which cell is the first figure, and which is the last?
Gadget is in row 3, and its figures run from column B to column D. A range joins its two corners with a colon. The Name Box accepts ranges too.
Type B3:D3 in the Name Box and press Enter. B3 is Gadget's January figure and D3 is its March figure, so the block between them is selected.
steps.explanation: Gadget's row is row 3. The range B3:D3 covers January, February and March, and nothing else.

common_mistakes.message: That selects only January. Add the end of the range after a colon.
That is Widget's row. Gadget is in row 3.
That includes the product name. Start at column B.

steps.prompt: The takings table ends at row 8. Add a label Total in column A of the next empty row, then press Enter.
hints: Where does the table end? What is the row number just below it?
The last day, Sunday, is in row 8, so the next empty row is row 9. The label belongs in column A, under the other days.
Click A9, type Total, and press Enter. Row 9 is the first empty row below the table, and column A holds the labels.
steps.explanation: The table's last row is 8, so the next empty row is 9. Labels sit in column A, so the cell is A9.

common_mistakes.message: That replaced Sunday's label. Use the empty row below the table.
That is the Takings column. The label belongs in column A.
A9 is still empty. Type Total and press Enter.

steps.prompt: Paper's price has risen to 6. Update it, and make sure the Item heading in A1 stays exactly as it is.
hints: Where will your typing go if you start typing right now?
Typing always goes into the active cell, the one with the thick green border. Right now that is A1, so move to Paper's price before you type.
Click B3 or type B3 in the Name Box and press Enter. Then type 6 and press Enter. Paper is row 3 and Price is column B.
steps.explanation: Typing replaces the active cell, which started as A1. Moving to B3 first protects the heading and changes Paper's price.

common_mistakes.message: You typed into A1 because it was still the active cell. Move to Paper's price first.
B3 still shows 5. Type 6 there and press Enter.
That is Pens' price. Paper is in row 3.

title: Cell Selection Shortcuts
objectives: By the end you can move the active cell with Tab, Enter and Home.
about: Moving around a worksheet with the keyboard is faster than using the mouse, especially for data entry. Tab moves the active cell one step right. Enter moves it one step down. Hold Shift with either key to go the opposite way, left or up. Home jumps to the start of the row, which is column A. Use these keys for timesheets, invoices, surveys, and any list you fill in or check row by row. To use them, click one cell to start, then press the key for the direction you want. Each press moves exactly one cell, except Home.

examples.scenario: A payroll clerk checks Amina's Tuesday hours on a timesheet.
examples.result: The active cell becomes C2, Tuesday's hours
examples.why: Each Tab moves one cell to the right.

examples.scenario: A bookkeeper steps down an invoice list.
examples.why: Each Enter moves one row down.

examples.scenario: A teacher goes back one column to fix a score.
examples.result: The active cell moves from C3 to B3
examples.why: Adding Shift reverses Tab, so it moves left.

examples.scenario: A researcher starts a survey sheet in column B and returns to the row start.
examples.result: The active cell moves from D2 to A2
examples.why: Home always goes to column A, even when column A is empty.

watch_out: Home goes to column A, not to the first cell that holds data.
Enter moves down by default. If it does not, the option may have been changed in Excel's settings.
recap: You can now move one cell at a time without touching the mouse. Next, the arrow keys will let you move faster.

steps.prompt: You are checking a timesheet and are on Amina's name in A2. Move to C2, her hours for Tuesday, using only the keyboard.
hints: Which key moves you one cell to the right? You need it twice.
Tab moves the active cell one cell to the right. Amina's name is in column A and Tuesday is in column C, so that is two cells to the right.
Press Tab twice. The active cell moves from A2 to B2, then to C2. Tab only ever moves one cell, so count the columns.
steps.explanation: Tab moves one cell right each time. Two presses take you from column A to column C.

common_mistakes.message: You moved only one cell. C2 is two cells right of A2.
Enter moves down, not right. Use Tab to move right.
One Tab too many. Tuesday is column C, and column D is Wednesday.

steps.prompt: You are checking invoices and are on INV-101's amount in C2. Move down to INV-104's amount using only the keyboard.
hints: Which key moves the active cell down? How many rows below INV-101 is INV-104?
Enter moves the active cell down one row. INV-104 is three rows below INV-101, so you need three presses.
Press Enter three times. The active cell moves from C2 to C3, C4, then C5, which is INV-104's amount.
steps.explanation: Enter moves down one row each time. Three presses take you from row 2 to row 5.

common_mistakes.message: You are one row short. INV-104 is in row 5.
Tab moves right. Use Enter to go down.
One Enter too many. INV-104 is in row 5, and row 6 is empty.

steps.prompt: You are on Tomas's Wednesday hours in D5. Go back to Priya's Monday hours in B4 using only the keyboard.
hints: You need one row up and two columns left. Which keys reverse Enter and Tab?
Hold Shift to reverse a key. Shift+Enter moves up one cell and Shift+Tab moves left one cell. You need one up and two lefts.
Press Shift+Enter once, then Shift+Tab twice. D5 moves to D4, C4, then B4, which is Priya's Monday hours.
steps.explanation: Shift reverses the direction. One Shift+Enter goes up a row and two Shift+Tab presses go back two columns.

common_mistakes.message: You went up but not left. B4 is two columns left of D.
That is Tomas's Monday. Priya is one row higher.
One Shift+Tab too many. Monday hours are in column B.

steps.prompt: You have reached the end of Daniel's row, at D3. Return to the start of that row, then move down to Priya's name.
hints: Which key jumps to the start of a row? Then which key moves down?
Home jumps to the first column of the row, which is column A. Enter then moves down one row. Priya is in the row below Daniel.
Press Home to reach A3, then press Enter to reach A4. A4 holds Priya's name.
steps.explanation: Home returns to column A in one press, and Enter moves down to the next person.

common_mistakes.message: You are at the start of Daniel's row. Move down one row to reach Priya.
That moved down but stayed in column D. Press Home first.
One Enter too many. Priya is in row 4.

steps.prompt: A survey sheet starts in column B, and you are at the end of row 9, in F9. Go to the very start of the row, down two rows, then one cell right to land on the response code in row 11.
hints: Which key goes to the start of a row? Check which column that is in this sheet.
Home goes to column A, even when column A is empty. Enter moves down and Tab moves one cell right. Count the rows and columns carefully.
Press Home, Enter, Enter, then Tab. Home lands on A9, two Enter presses reach A11, and Tab moves to B11.
steps.explanation: Home always goes to column A, which is empty here. From A9, two Enter presses reach A11, and Tab moves to B11.

common_mistakes.message: You counted from column B, but Home goes to column A. A11 plus one Tab is B11.
You stopped one key short. Press Tab to move one cell right.
You pressed Enter only once. Two rows down from row 9 is row 11.

title: Arrow Keys
objectives: By the end you can move one cell with an arrow key and jump to the edge of a block of data with Ctrl+Arrow.
about: Arrow keys move the active cell one step at a time, in the direction of the arrow. Hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and they jump instead. A jump lands on the last filled cell of a block. If you start at the end of a block, it crosses empty cells to the next filled one. One key press then replaces scrolling through hundreds of rows. Use it to find the end of a list or the edge of a table. To use it, click a cell in the data, hold Ctrl, and tap an arrow.

shortcut_table.action: Jump to the edge of a data block

examples.scenario: A shop owner walks down a stock list one item at a time.
examples.result: The active cell moves from B2 to B4, Tape's stock
examples.why: Each arrow press moves one cell.

examples.scenario: An accountant finds the last invoice in a long list.
examples.result: The active cell jumps from A1 to A6
examples.why: The jump stops on the last filled cell before an empty one.

examples.scenario: An analyst finds the last column of a report heading.
examples.result: The active cell jumps from A1 to D1
examples.why: The same jump works across a row.

examples.scenario: A clerk faces a list with one deleted entry.
examples.result: From A4 the active cell jumps to A6
examples.why: From the end of a block, the jump crosses the empty cell and lands on the next filled one.

watch_out: A blank cell stops the jump. If you land short of where you expected, there is a gap in the data.
On a Mac, use Cmd+Arrow. Ctrl+Arrow is often taken by Mission Control.
recap: Ctrl+Arrow now takes you to the edge of any block of data. Next, you will use Shift with the arrows to select cells.

steps.prompt: Your stock list is open on Pens' stock in B2. Walk down with the arrow key to Glue's stock in B5.
hints: Which key moves the active cell down one row? How many rows is Glue below Pens?
The Down arrow moves the active cell one row at a time. Glue is three rows below Pens, so press the Down arrow three times.
Press the Down arrow three times. B2 moves to B3, B4, then B5, which holds Glue's stock, 12.
steps.explanation: Each arrow press moves exactly one cell in its direction. Three presses take you from Pens to Glue.

common_mistakes.message: You are one row short. Glue is in row 5.
That is past the data. Stock is in column B.
One press too many. That is Clips' stock.

steps.prompt: You are in A1 on an order list. Jump straight to the last order number in column A.
hints: Which key combination jumps to the end of a block of data? Think arrow key plus a modifier.
Hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and press the Down arrow. Excel jumps to the last filled cell below you, instead of moving one cell.
Press Ctrl+Down once (Cmd+Down on a Mac). The active cell jumps from A1 to A8, the last order in the list.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+Down travels down a block of filled cells and stops on the last one before a blank.

common_mistakes.message: The arrow alone moves one cell. Hold Ctrl so it jumps to the end of the data.
That jumped right along the header row. You need Down.
A second jump ran past the end of the data to the bottom of the sheet. One press was enough.

steps.prompt: You are on the first heading, Order, in A1. Jump to the last heading in the row to see which columns the export has.
hints: The headings run across a row. Which jump key follows them to the end?
Hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) and press the Right arrow. Excel jumps along the row to the last filled heading before an empty cell.
Press Ctrl+Right once. The active cell jumps from A1 to D1, the Amount heading.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+Right runs along a row of filled cells and stops on the last one.

common_mistakes.message: One arrow press moves one cell. Add Ctrl to jump to the end of the row.
That jumped down the column. You need Right.
That also went down. Only the heading row was needed.

steps.prompt: You are on the Total for Doohickey in F6, the bottom-right of a report. Jump back to the top-left corner of the table, the Product heading in B2.
hints: You need to travel up and left to the corner. Which two jumps get you there?
Ctrl with an arrow jumps to the edge of the data in that direction. Use Up for the top row and Left for the first column, in either order.
Press Ctrl+Up, then Ctrl+Left. F6 jumps to F2, then to B2, the Product heading. Cmd instead of Ctrl on a Mac.
steps.explanation: Two jumps in two directions reach the corner of the table.

common_mistakes.message: You reached the top row but still need to go left.
You reached the first column but still need to go up.
One jump too many ran past the heading to the top of the sheet.

steps.prompt: You are in A2 on a long order list. One order number was deleted, leaving a gap. Reach the very last order at the bottom.
hints: A blank cell stops the jump. How many presses will you need?
Ctrl+Down stops just above a blank cell. Press it again to cross the gap, then once more to reach the end of the second block.
Press Ctrl+Down three times. The active cell stops at A5, then crosses the gap to A7, then runs to A10.
steps.explanation: The first jump stops at A5, above the blank in A6. The second crosses the gap to A7. The third runs to A10.

common_mistakes.message: You stopped just before the blank in A6. Press again to cross it.
You crossed the gap but are not at the end yet. One more jump.
Four jumps ran past the data to the bottom of the sheet. Three are enough.

title: Larger Cell Selections
objectives: By the end you can select a block of cells using Shift+Arrow and Ctrl+Shift+Arrow.
about: Before you can format, copy, or add up cells, you have to select them. Selecting means highlighting one or more cells so Excel knows which ones you mean. Hold Shift and press an arrow key to grow the selection one cell at a time. Add Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) to grow it to the end of a block of data. Use this to highlight a column of figures, a heading row, or a whole table. To use it, click the first cell, hold Shift, and press the arrow keys. Press an arrow without Shift to start again.

shortcut_table.action: Extend to the end of the data

examples.scenario: A teacher highlights Amina's three scores.
examples.why: Each press adds one cell to the selection.

examples.scenario: A shop owner selects a column of monthly sales.
examples.why: The selection stops on the last filled cell.

examples.scenario: An office manager selects a whole staff table to copy.
examples.why: Two jumps cover the width and the height.

examples.scenario: A shop owner selects too many months and fixes it.
examples.why: The opposite arrow shrinks the selection back toward the starting cell.

watch_out: The selection grows from the cell where you started. The opposite arrow shrinks it again.
A blank cell stops Ctrl+Shift+Arrow, just as it stops Ctrl+Arrow.
recap: You can now select any block from the keyboard. Next, you will select whole rows and columns.

steps.prompt: Your monthly sales are listed in column B. Starting on February (B3), select the sales for February to May.
hints: Which key adds 'extend the selection' to an arrow? How many cells below February do you need?
Hold Shift and press the Down arrow to grow the selection one cell per press. February to May is four cells, so three presses after the first.
Press Shift+Down three times. The selection grows from B3 to B3:B6, covering February, March, April and May.
steps.explanation: Shift keeps the starting cell fixed and grows the selection one cell per arrow press.

common_mistakes.message: You are one cell short. May is in row 6.
Shift+Right extends sideways. Use Shift+Down.
One press too many. June is not part of this request.

steps.prompt: You are on Leeds's February figure in C2. Select the block C2:E4: Leeds, Bristol and Derby for February to April.
hints: Count how many extra columns and rows you must add beyond the starting cell.
Hold Shift and press Right twice, then Down twice. The order does not matter, because the selection grows from C2 either way.
Press Shift+Right twice and Shift+Down twice. C2 grows to C2:E4, a block three columns wide and three rows tall.
steps.explanation: The block is three columns wide and three rows tall, so each direction needs two extra presses.

common_mistakes.message: You covered the width but not the height.
You covered the height but not the width.
One Shift+Right too many. The block ends in column E.

steps.prompt: You want to colour the heading row of the store report. You are on Store in A1. Select the whole row of headings, from Store to May, with one jump.
hints: You want the selection to run to the end of the headings in one move. Which keys do that?
Hold Ctrl and Shift together and press Right. The selection grows from your cell to the last filled cell in the row (Cmd+Shift on a Mac).
Press Ctrl+Shift+Right once. The selection grows from A1 to A1:F1, covering every heading up to May.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+Shift+Right grows the selection to the end of the block in one press.

common_mistakes.message: That stops short. A jump selects the whole row of headings.
That selected downward. Headings run across the row.
You also extended down. Only the heading row was needed.

steps.prompt: You are on the Item heading in B3 of a stock report. Select the whole table, headings included, so you can copy it.
hints: The table has a width and a height. Which jumps cover each?
Use Ctrl+Shift+Right to cover the width and Ctrl+Shift+Down to cover the height, in either order. The title in B1 is not part of the table.
Press Ctrl+Shift+Right, then Ctrl+Shift+Down. The selection grows from B3 to B3:E3, then down to B3:E10.
steps.explanation: Two jumps with Shift select the width and the height. The title in row 1 stays outside the selection.

common_mistakes.message: You covered the width only. Now extend downward.
You covered the height only. Now extend to the right.
Two presses of Ctrl+A would select the whole sheet. Use jumps to select just the table.

steps.prompt: You are in B2 on a column of order amounts. One amount is missing. Select every amount down to the last filled cell, B9.
hints: A blank cell stops the selection jump. How many presses might you need?
Ctrl+Shift+Down stops just above a blank. Press it again to cross the gap, and once more to reach the end of the second block.
Press Ctrl+Shift+Down three times. The selection reaches B5, then B7 after the gap, then B9 at the end.
steps.explanation: Each press grows the selection to the next edge. The blank in B6 splits the column into two blocks, so it takes three presses.

common_mistakes.message: You stopped above the blank in B6. Press again to cross it.
You crossed the gap but not the second block. One more press.
Too many presses ran past the data to the bottom of the sheet.

title: Row and Column Selections
objectives: By the end you can select whole rows and columns with Shift+Space and Ctrl+Space.
about: Sometimes you need a whole row or column, for example to colour a heading or delete a column. Shift+Space selects the whole row that holds the active cell. Ctrl+Space selects the whole column. Add Shift with an arrow key to widen the selection to neighbouring rows or columns. Use them to format, insert, hide or delete rows and columns quickly. To use them, click any cell in the row or column you want, then press the shortcut. On a Mac, use Control+Space for the column. It may clash with a system setting that switches the keyboard language.

examples.scenario: A manager removes a cancelled order from the list.
examples.result: Row 4 is selected from end to end
examples.why: Shift+Space selects the whole row of the active cell.

examples.scenario: A bookkeeper wants to format every amount.
examples.result: Column C is selected from top to bottom
examples.why: Ctrl+Space selects the whole column of the active cell.

examples.scenario: A teacher widens a column selection to include Science.
examples.result: Columns B and C are selected
examples.why: Shift with an arrow widens the selection one column at a time.

examples.scenario: An analyst wants columns B to D but starts in column C.
examples.result: Columns B to D are selected
examples.why: A selection grows one way from its start, so begin in the first column you want.

watch_out: The selection grows in one direction from where you started. To select columns B to D, start in B.
On a Mac, Control+Space may switch your keyboard language. If it does, turn that system shortcut off in System Settings.
recap: You can now select whole rows and columns quickly. Next, you will use Ctrl+Home, Ctrl+End and Go To to travel across a sheet.

steps.prompt: Order ORD-1003 was cancelled and its whole row must be deleted. You are on its Region cell, B4. Select the entire row.
hints: Which shortcut selects an entire row? It pairs Shift with the longest key on the keyboard.
Shift+Space selects the whole row that holds the active cell, from column A to the end of the sheet, whichever column you are in.
Press Shift+Space once. Row 4 is highlighted from column A across, so the whole row is selected and ready to delete.
steps.explanation: Shift+Space selects the row that holds the active cell, whichever column you start in.

common_mistakes.message: That selected the column. Use Shift+Space for the row.
That selected three cells, not the whole row.
You widened to two rows. Stop after Shift+Space.

steps.prompt: The Amount column needs a currency format. You are on ORD-1002's amount in D3. Select the whole column.
hints: A whole column is the vertical partner of a whole row. Which shortcut selects it?
Ctrl+Space selects the whole column that holds the active cell, from row 1 to the bottom of the sheet (Control+Space on a Mac).
Press Ctrl+Space once. Column D, the Amount column, is highlighted from the top of the sheet to the bottom.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+Space selects the column that holds the active cell, so every amount, including future ones, is covered.

common_mistakes.message: That selected the row. Columns use Ctrl+Space.
That selects only down to the last filled cell. Ctrl+Space takes the whole column.
Shift+Left widened to the left. Only column D was needed.

steps.prompt: You are on Bristol's January figure in B3. Select the January and February columns together so you can set their width.
hints: Start with one whole column, then widen. Which keys do each job?
Select the column first, then add the neighbour. Shift with an arrow key widens a column selection by one column at a time.
Press Ctrl+Space to select column B, then Shift+Right to add column C. Columns B and C are now selected.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+Space selects January's column. Shift+Right adds February's column beside it.

common_mistakes.message: That is only January. Widen it with Shift+Right.
Shift+Left widened to the left. February is on the right.
One widen too many. March is not part of this request.

steps.prompt: Three rows of the store report are no longer needed: rows 3, 4 and 5. You are on a cell in row 3, C3. Select all three rows together.
hints: Select one whole row first, then grow the selection downward.
Shift+Space selects the row. Shift+Down then widens the selection by one whole row each time. Rows 3 to 5 need two widens.
Press Shift+Space, then Shift+Down twice. The selection grows from row 3 to rows 3, 4 and 5.
steps.explanation: Shift+Space selects row 3. Each Shift+Down adds the whole row below it.

common_mistakes.message: That is only row 3. Widen it with Shift+Down.
You are one row short. Row 5 is also needed.
One widen too many. Row 6 is not part of this request.

steps.prompt: You are on ORD-1004's rep in C5, in the middle of the table. Select the Region, Rep and Amount columns together.
hints: A selection grows in one direction from where you start. Where should you start?
Start in the first column you want, column B. Select it with Ctrl+Space, then widen to the right until column D is included.
Press Left to reach B5, then Ctrl+Space to select column B. Press Shift+Right twice to add columns C and D.
steps.explanation: A selection grows only one way from its starting column. Starting in B lets you widen right to D.

common_mistakes.message: Shift+Left then Shift+Right shrinks back to C. Start in column B instead.
You started in C, so you can only grow to the right from there.
One Shift+Right short. Column D is still missing.

title: Cell Selection Shortcuts 2
objectives: By the end you can jump to A1, to the last used cell, or to any address from the keyboard.
about: Large worksheets can run to hundreds of rows, so you need fast ways to travel. Ctrl+Home takes you straight to cell A1. Ctrl+End takes you to the last cell that holds data. Ctrl+G opens the Go To box, where you type any address, even a block like B2:D9. Use them to return to the top or to check where a sheet really ends. They also help when a colleague says, look at cell J20. To use them, press the shortcut. For Go To, type the address and press Enter, and Excel jumps there at once.

shortcut_table.action: Go to the last used cell

examples.scenario: An analyst returns to the top of a stock list.
examples.result: The active cell jumps from C6 to A1
examples.why: It always returns to the top-left corner.

examples.scenario: An auditor checks where the same list ends.
examples.result: The active cell jumps from A1 to C6
examples.why: Ctrl+End goes to the last used row and the last used column.

examples.scenario: A clerk must reach a cell a colleague mentioned.
examples.result: The active cell moves to J20
examples.why: Go To jumps to any address you type.

examples.scenario: An office worker finds a stray note that stretches the sheet.
examples.result: The active cell jumps from A1 to D5
examples.why: A stray entry or old formatting stretches the used area. Ctrl+End reveals it.

watch_out: Ctrl+End goes to the last used cell, which can look empty. Stray entries move it.
Go To accepts any address, such as J20, and also ranges, such as B2:D9.
recap: You can now cross any sheet in a few key presses. Next, you will combine these jumps with Shift to select large areas.

steps.prompt: You have been checking prices deep in a stock list and are now in F9. Return to the very top-left cell of the sheet in one move.
hints: One shortcut returns you to A1 from anywhere. Its key name means 'start'.
Hold Ctrl and press Home to jump to cell A1 from any position, however far down or across you are. On a Mac, use Fn+Control+Left.
Press Ctrl+Home. The active cell jumps from F9 to A1. Plain Home would only take you to column A in the same row.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+Home always returns to A1, wherever you are on the sheet.

common_mistakes.message: Home stays in the same row. Ctrl+Home goes all the way to A1.
That jumped up the column but stayed in column F.
Ctrl+End goes to the opposite corner, the last used cell.

steps.prompt: Your stock list has been growing all year. You are on A1. Jump to the last cell that holds data to see where the list ends.
hints: There is a shortcut for the opposite corner from A1. Which key means 'end'?
Hold Ctrl and press End. Excel jumps to the last used row and the last used column together, which is the bottom-right of your data.
Press Ctrl+End. The active cell jumps from A1 to F12, the last cell of the list. On a Mac, use Fn+Control+Right.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+End goes to the last row and last column that hold data, which is F12 here.

common_mistakes.message: That reached the last row only. Ctrl+End also goes to the last column.
That reached the last column only. Ctrl+End also goes to the last row.

steps.prompt: A colleague says the supplier note is in cell J20, far off screen. You are on A1. Use the keyboard to go to J20.
hints: You need a shortcut that takes you to an address you type. Which one is it?
Ctrl+G opens the Go To box (F5 does too). Type the address you want in the box, then press Enter to jump there.
Press Ctrl+G, type J20, then press Enter. The active cell jumps straight to J20, however far away it is.
steps.explanation: Go To accepts any address and jumps there at once, however far away it is.

common_mistakes.message: The box needs Enter to confirm. Type J20, then press Enter.
That address is in column A. Check the letter in J20.

steps.prompt: You want to format every figure in the order list without dragging. Use Go To to select the block from B2 to D9.
hints: Go To accepts more than one cell. What can you type to name a whole block?
Ctrl+G opens the Go To box. Type a range with a colon, such as B2:D9, and press Enter. Excel selects the whole block at once.
Press Ctrl+G, type B2:D9, then press Enter. The block from B2 down to D9 is selected without any dragging.
steps.explanation: Go To accepts a range as well as a single cell. Typing B2:D9 selects that block in one step.

common_mistakes.message: That went to one cell. Type the whole range, B2:D9.
That went to the last cell only. Type the whole range, with a colon.
The range stopped one row early. The last order is in row 9.

steps.prompt: The order list ends at D8, yet the file feels heavy. You are in B3. Jump to the last cell Excel counts as used to find out why.
hints: The corner Excel counts as used may not be the corner of the table. Which shortcut finds it?
Ctrl+End goes to the last used row and the last used column of the whole sheet, including stray entries far from the table.
Press Ctrl+End. You land on G12, where a stray note sits. That note stretches the sheet far beyond the table.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+End uses the last row and last column that hold data. The stray note in G12 pushes that corner past the table.

common_mistakes.message: That is the corner of the table, not the last used cell. Ctrl+End also counts stray entries.
That is the opposite corner. Use Ctrl+End.
That only reaches the bottom of column B. Ctrl+End covers the whole sheet.

title: Larger Cell Selections 2
objectives: By the end you can select to the last used cell, back to A1, or the whole data block with Ctrl+Shift+End, Ctrl+Shift+Home and Ctrl+A.
about: Once you can jump around a sheet, you can select as far as you can jump. Ctrl+Shift+End selects from your cell to the last used cell. Ctrl+Shift+Home selects back to A1. Ctrl+A selects the whole block of data around you. Pressing it a second time selects the entire sheet. Use these before copying a table, formatting everything, or checking how far a sheet really reaches. Each one saves you from dragging the mouse across a large table. To use them, click a cell first, because the selection starts from the cell you are on.

shortcut_table.action: Select to the last used cell
Select the data block, then the sheet

examples.scenario: A clerk selects a product table to copy it.
examples.why: One press selects the table around the active cell.

examples.scenario: A teacher wants to change the font everywhere.
examples.result: Every cell in the sheet is selected
examples.why: A second press goes from the table to the whole sheet.

examples.scenario: An analyst selects from a score back to the top.
examples.why: The selection grows from the active cell back to A1.

examples.scenario: An office worker finds a stray entry that stretches the sheet.
examples.why: The last used cell is D5, not B3.

watch_out: Ctrl+Shift+End reaches the last used cell, which may lie beyond the visible data.
Ctrl+A inside a table selects the table only. Press it again for the whole sheet.
recap: You can now select to any corner of a sheet. Next, a summary lesson will mix all the selection shortcuts.

steps.prompt: You are in B3 inside a small product table. Copy the whole table by first selecting it with one shortcut.
hints: One shortcut selects the whole block of data around you. It uses the first letter of the alphabet.
Ctrl+A selects the block of data around the active cell, as long as you are inside it (Cmd+A on a Mac).
Press Ctrl+A once. The table A1:C6 is selected, headings included. A second press would select the whole sheet.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+A first selects the block of data around the active cell. A second press would select the whole sheet.

common_mistakes.message: Two presses selected the whole sheet. One press is enough to select the table.
That selected only from B3 back to A1. Ctrl+A takes the whole table.
That went to the last used cell. Ctrl+A selects the whole table.

steps.prompt: You are on ORD-1004's rep in C5. Select everything from here back to the top-left cell, A1.
hints: You want to extend your selection all the way back to the start of the sheet.
Ctrl+Shift+Home extends the selection from your cell to A1. The corner you started in stays fixed, and the rest grows towards the top.
Press Ctrl+Shift+Home. The selection grows from C5 back to A1, covering A1:C5.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+Shift+Home grows the selection from the active cell back to A1.

common_mistakes.message: Ctrl+A selects the whole table, not just back to A1.
That went the other way, to the last used cell.
Ctrl+Home moves without selecting. Add Shift.

steps.prompt: You are on the first region in B2 and want everything from there to the end of the order list. Select down to the last used cell.
hints: One shortcut selects from your cell to the far corner of your data. Which key means 'end'?
Ctrl+Shift+End extends the selection from your cell to the last used cell of the sheet. On a Mac, use Fn+Control+Shift+Right.
Press Ctrl+Shift+End. The selection grows from B2 to the last used cell, D9, covering B2:D9.
steps.explanation: The last used cell is D9, so the selection runs from B2 to that corner.

common_mistakes.message: You covered the width only. Ctrl+Shift+End also covers the height.
You covered the height only. Ctrl+Shift+End also covers the width.
That went back to A1. You want the opposite corner.

steps.prompt: You want to change the font of every cell in the sheet. You are in B3 inside the table. Select the entire sheet.
hints: One shortcut selects the table. Pressed again, it selects something bigger.
Ctrl+A selects the block of data around you. Press it a second time to select every cell in the sheet.
Press Ctrl+A twice. The first press selects the table, and the second selects the whole sheet.
steps.explanation: The first Ctrl+A selects the table, and the second goes from the table to the entire sheet.

common_mistakes.message: One press selects only the table. Press Ctrl+A again.
That selected to the last used cell, not the whole sheet.

steps.prompt: You are in B2 on an order list. A stray note sits far from the table. Select from B2 to the last used cell, wherever it is.
hints: The last used cell may not be the corner of the table. Which shortcut reaches it?
Ctrl+Shift+End extends the selection to the last used cell, including stray entries (Fn+Control+Shift+Right on a Mac).
Press Ctrl+Shift+End. The selection runs from B2 to H12, where a stray note sits, because that is the last used cell.
steps.explanation: The last used cell is H12, because the stray note sits in column H and row 12. The selection runs from B2 to that corner.

common_mistakes.message: That stopped at the table. A stray note makes H12 the last used cell.
That went back to A1. You want the opposite corner.
Two presses of Ctrl+A select the whole sheet, which is more than the task asks.

title: Cell Selection Skill Summary
objectives: By the end you can combine jumping, selecting and Go To without the mouse.
about: This lesson mixes every selection shortcut from lessons 01 to 07, so there is no new material, only practice. In real work you rarely use one shortcut alone. You jump to the data, select it, then move on. Your job here is to choose the shortest route each time. Use this lesson to find the shortcuts you still replace with the mouse. To use it, read each problem, decide which keys fit, and try the shortest path. If a shortcut lands somewhere unexpected, look for blank cells in the data.

shortcut_table.action: Jump to the edge of data
Extend to the edge of data
Go to A1 / last used cell
Select to A1 / last used cell
Select the data block, then the sheet

examples.scenario: A stock clerk wants to find the end of a list.
examples.result: The active cell moves from A1 to D4
examples.why: Two jumps reach the far corner of the data.

examples.scenario: The clerk then selects the list to copy it.
examples.why: Ctrl+Shift+Home grows the selection from D4 back to A1.

examples.scenario: The clerk selects two rows to delete them.
examples.why: Select one row, then widen by one.

examples.scenario: A manager asks for a block far down the sheet to be selected.
examples.why: Go To takes a range as well as a cell.

watch_out: When a shortcut lands somewhere unexpected, look for blank cells in the data.
Pick the shortest sequence. Two jumps usually beat ten arrow presses.
recap: You now have a full toolkit for moving and selecting. Next, you will meet the shortcuts that undo, redo and edit.

steps.prompt: You open a stock list and want to see how long it is. From A1, jump to its bottom-right cell.
hints: Two jumps in two directions reach the corner. Which keys jump to the edge of data?
Hold Ctrl (Cmd on a Mac) with an arrow key to jump to the edge of the data. Use Right for the last column and Down for the last row.
Press Ctrl+Right, then Ctrl+Down. A1 jumps to E1, then to E12, the bottom-right cell of the list.
steps.explanation: Each Ctrl+Arrow runs to the edge of the data block. Two jumps reach the corner.

common_mistakes.message: You reached the last column. Now jump down.
You reached the last row. Now jump right.
A third jump ran past the data to the bottom of the sheet.

steps.prompt: You are on the last cell of the stock list, E12. Select the whole list back to A1 so you can copy it.
hints: You want to extend your selection back to the start of the sheet.
Ctrl+Shift+Home extends the selection from your cell to A1, covering everything between the two corners.
Press Ctrl+Shift+Home. The selection grows from E12 back to A1, covering the whole list, A1:E12.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+Shift+Home grows the selection from the active cell back to A1, covering the whole list.

common_mistakes.message: Ctrl+Home moves without selecting. Add Shift.
That selected one row only. Ctrl+Shift+Home reaches A1.
That selected only column E. Ctrl+Shift+Home reaches A1.

steps.prompt: Two rows of the stock list were entered twice. You are on C4. Select rows 4 and 5 together so you can delete them.
hints: Select one whole row first, then widen by one row.
Shift+Space selects the row of the active cell. Shift+Down then adds the whole row below it to the selection.
Press Shift+Space, then Shift+Down. Rows 4 and 5 are selected together and ready to delete.
steps.explanation: Shift+Space selects row 4. Shift+Down widens the selection by one whole row.

common_mistakes.message: That is only row 4. Widen it with Shift+Down.
Shift+Up widened upward. You need the row below.
That selected the column. Rows use Shift+Space.

steps.prompt: Your manager wants Item 10's category, quantity and price highlighted. They sit in B11 to D11. From A1, travel there and select them.
hints: Travel first, then select. Which shortcut travels to an address you type?
Ctrl+G opens Go To. After it takes you to B11, Shift+Right extends the selection one cell at a time to the right.
Press Ctrl+G, type B11, press Enter. Then press Shift+Right twice. The selection grows from B11 to B11:D11.
steps.explanation: Go To lands you on B11. Two Shift+Right presses then extend the selection to D11.

common_mistakes.message: You reached B11 but did not select. Add two Shift+Right presses.
One Shift+Right short. D11 is still outside the selection.
The box needs Enter to confirm the address.

steps.prompt: You are in A1. The sheet has a regional table, a blank row, and a Total row. Select all of it, Total row included.
hints: A blank row stops the selection jump. Think about how many presses that costs you.
Select across with Ctrl+Shift+Right. Then press Ctrl+Shift+Down once to stop above the blank row, and once more to cross it.
Press Ctrl+Shift+Right, then Ctrl+Shift+Down twice. The first Down stops at row 8, the second reaches row 10.
steps.explanation: The first downward jump stops at row 8, above the blank row. The second crosses the gap and reaches the Total row in row 10.

common_mistakes.message: The blank row 9 stopped the selection. Press Ctrl+Shift+Down again to cross it.
You covered the width only. Now extend downward.
One press too many ran past the Total row to the bottom of the sheet.

title: Intro to Shortcuts
objectives: By the end you can undo, redo, edit and cancel without the mouse.
about: A shortcut is a key combination that does in one press what would take several mouse clicks. The four in this lesson fix mistakes. Ctrl+Z undoes your last action. Ctrl+Y redoes what you just undid. F2 puts the active cell into edit mode. You can then change part of its contents instead of replacing it. Esc cancels an entry you have typed but not yet saved. Use them whenever you type the wrong thing or want to adjust a long entry. To use them, press the key combination while the sheet is active. On a Mac, Cmd replaces Ctrl.

examples.scenario: A shop owner types a wrong price and undoes it.
examples.why: Undo reverses your last action.

examples.scenario: The owner changes her mind again and redoes it.
examples.why: Redo restores what you just undid.

examples.scenario: A clerk starts typing in the wrong cell and backs out.
examples.why: Esc cancels an entry that has not been saved. After Enter, use Ctrl+Z instead.

examples.scenario: A manager adds a word to a long note.
examples.why: F2 edits the existing text. Typing straight in would replace it.

watch_out: Typing straight into a cell replaces what is there. Press F2 first to edit the existing text.
Undo works step by step, and a new action clears the redo history.
recap: You can now fix mistakes without reaching for the mouse. Next, you will format text from the keyboard.

steps.prompt: You pasted the wrong figures into your report. Press the shortcut that undoes your last action.
hints: Which key combination reverses your last action? It uses the last letter of the alphabet.
Ctrl+Z undoes the last thing you did, such as a paste or a typed value. You can press it again to go back further. On a Mac, use Cmd+Z.
Press Ctrl+Z (Cmd+Z on a Mac). Your last action is reversed. Pressing it again undoes the action before that one.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+Z undoes your last action, and repeated presses step further back.

common_mistakes.message: Ctrl+Y redoes an action. Undo is Ctrl+Z.
Ctrl+C copies. Undo is Ctrl+Z.

steps.prompt: You are updating the price of pens, 50 in B2. Change it to 60 and press Enter, then change it to 70 and press Enter. Your manager says the first change was right: undo once so B2 shows 60.
hints: Make both changes first. Then which key undoes only the last one?
Type each value and press Enter. Ctrl+Z reverses one action at a time, so a single press cancels the 70 but keeps the 60 (Cmd+Z on a Mac).
Type 60 and press Enter. Press Shift+Enter to go back up to B2, type 70 and press Enter, then press Ctrl+Z once. B2 returns to 60.
steps.explanation: Each Ctrl+Z reverses one action. One press cancels the change to 70 and leaves the earlier change to 60.

common_mistakes.message: B2 shows 70. Undo once with Ctrl+Z to return to 60.
You undid both changes. One Ctrl+Z reverses one action.

steps.prompt: Pens stock is 50 in B2. You type a new count of 500 and press Enter. A colleague says it was wrong, so you undo it. Then she says it was right after all. Finish with B2 showing 500.
hints: Which shortcut brings back something you have just undone?
Ctrl+Y redoes an action you undid with Ctrl+Z. It only works until you make a new change. On a Mac, use Cmd+Y.
Type 500 and press Enter. Press Ctrl+Z to undo it, so B2 shows 50. Then press Ctrl+Y to redo it, and B2 shows 500 again.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+Z reverses the entry and Ctrl+Y restores it, so B2 ends on 500.

common_mistakes.message: B2 is back at 50. Redo the entry with Ctrl+Y to restore 500.
Use both Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y so you practise undo and redo.

steps.prompt: You start typing a new quantity, 99, into D4 but realise it is the wrong cell. Cancel the entry so D4 still shows 45.
hints: Your entry is not saved yet. Which key cancels it?
Esc cancels an entry before you press Enter, so the cell keeps its old value. After Enter, you would need Ctrl+Z instead.
Type 99, then press Esc instead of Enter. D4 keeps showing 45 because the entry was cancelled before it was saved.
steps.explanation: Esc cancels an entry that has not been saved yet. Once you press Enter, you would need Ctrl+Z instead.

common_mistakes.message: Enter saved the 99. Press Esc instead to cancel, or Ctrl+Z to undo it.
Delete cleared the cell. Esc cancels an entry without changing the cell.

steps.prompt: Cell E2 says Sale Pending. Without retyping the whole note, add an exclamation mark to the end.
hints: Typing straight into a cell replaces it. How can you edit what is already there?
F2 puts the cell into edit mode with the cursor at the end of the text, so what you type is added instead of replacing it. Control+U on a Mac.
Press F2, type !, then press Enter. The cursor starts at the end of the text, so the exclamation mark is added to Sale Pending.
steps.explanation: F2 opens the existing text for editing, so what you type is added to the end instead of replacing it.

common_mistakes.message: Typing straight away replaced the whole cell. Press F2 first so you edit the existing text.
You opened the cell but did not add the exclamation mark.

title: Text Formatting Shortcuts
objectives: By the end you can bold, italicise, underline and strike through cells from the keyboard.
about: Formatting makes important cells easy to spot, such as headings, totals, and corrections. These shortcuts apply the most common text formats without opening the ribbon. Ctrl+B makes text bold. Ctrl+I makes it italic. Ctrl+U underlines it. Ctrl+5 adds a strikethrough, a line through the text. Pressing the same shortcut again turns the format off. Use them on headings, totals, and cancelled items, so readers notice what matters. To use them, select the cell or cells first, then press the shortcut. On a Mac, use Cmd instead of Ctrl, and Cmd+Shift+X for strikethrough.

examples.scenario: An accountant makes invoice headings stand out.
examples.why: The shortcut formats everything selected.

examples.scenario: A clerk marks a cancelled order.
examples.why: Strikethrough shows a cancellation without deleting the entry.

examples.scenario: A manager highlights the Total label.
examples.why: Several formats can sit on one cell.

examples.scenario: A bookkeeper removes bold that was added by mistake.
examples.result: The bold is removed when the cell was already bold
examples.why: The shortcuts toggle. A second press turns the format off.

watch_out: Each shortcut is a toggle. If a cell is already formatted, the same shortcut removes the format.
Select the cells first. The shortcut formats whatever is selected.
recap: You can now format text without the ribbon. Next, you will enter dates, times and multi-line text quickly.

steps.prompt: You are building an invoice. Make the three headings in A1:C1 bold so they stand out. You are on A1.
hints: Select the three headings first, then apply the format. Which keys do each job?
Shift+Right twice selects A1:C1. Ctrl+B then makes everything selected bold (Cmd+B on a Mac). Pressing it again would turn bold off.
Press Shift+Right twice to select A1:C1, then press Ctrl+B. All three headings become bold at once.
steps.explanation: The shortcut formats whatever is selected, so selecting the row first makes all three headings bold at once.

common_mistakes.message: Only A1 became bold. Select A1:C1 first with Shift+Right.
You selected only two headings. Press Shift+Right twice.
That is italic. Bold is Ctrl+B.

steps.prompt: Order ORD-1004 was cancelled. You are on its order number in A5. Mark it with strikethrough and italic, without deleting it.
hints: Two separate formats are needed. One of them uses a number key.
Ctrl+5 adds strikethrough, a line through the text (Cmd+Shift+X on a Mac). Ctrl+I adds italic. Each shortcut adds one format to the selected cell.
Press Ctrl+5 for the strikethrough, then Ctrl+I for the italic. The order number is crossed out and slanted but still readable.
steps.explanation: Each shortcut adds one format. Strikethrough marks the order as cancelled without deleting it.

common_mistakes.message: Strikethrough is on, but the task also asks for italic. Add Ctrl+I.
Italic is on, but the cancellation needs strikethrough. Use Ctrl+5.
Ctrl+U underlines. Strikethrough is Ctrl+5.

steps.prompt: The sales sheet ends with a Total row. You are on the Total label in A6. Make it bold and underlined so it stands out.
hints: Bold and underline are two separate formats. Which shortcut starts each one?
Ctrl+B makes the text bold and Ctrl+U underlines it. Apply both to the same cell. Cmd+B and Cmd+U on a Mac.
Press Ctrl+B, then Ctrl+U. The Total label becomes bold and underlined, so it stands out from the month rows.
steps.explanation: Both formats can sit on the same cell, so one shortcut for each is enough.

common_mistakes.message: Bold is on, but the label is not underlined yet. Add Ctrl+U.
Underline is on, but the label is not bold yet. Add Ctrl+B.
Ctrl+I is italic. Bold is Ctrl+B and underline is Ctrl+U.

steps.prompt: Three monthly sales figures in B2 to B4 are only estimates. Mark them italic. You are on B2.
hints: Select all three figures before you format. Which keys select them, and which make italic?
Shift+Down twice selects B2:B4. Ctrl+I then makes every selected cell italic, so one shortcut covers all three (Cmd+I on a Mac).
Press Shift+Down twice to select B2:B4, then press Ctrl+I. The three estimates slant to the right.
steps.explanation: Selecting first means one Ctrl+I formats all three cells at once.

common_mistakes.message: Only B2 became italic. Select B2:B4 first with Shift+Down.
B4 was left out. Three cells need two Shift+Down presses.
That is bold. Italic is Ctrl+I.

steps.prompt: B2 was made bold by mistake. Remove the bold and underline it instead. You are on B2.
hints: These shortcuts switch a format on or off. What happens when it is already on?
Ctrl+B turns bold off when the cell is already bold. Ctrl+U adds underline. Press each once (Cmd on a Mac).
Press Ctrl+B to remove the bold, then Ctrl+U to underline. B2 ends underlined and no longer bold.
steps.explanation: Each shortcut is a toggle. Because B2 was already bold, Ctrl+B switched bold off.

common_mistakes.message: B2 is still bold. Ctrl+B turns bold off because it is already on.
Bold is off but B2 is not underlined yet. Add Ctrl+U.

title: Data Shortcuts
objectives: By the end you can enter dates and times, start a new line in a cell, and fill a selection with one entry.
about: Data-entry shortcuts save typing and prevent mistakes. Ctrl+; enters today's date. Ctrl+Shift+; enters the current time. Alt+Enter starts a new line inside a cell. Ctrl+Enter fills your entry into every selected cell at once. Logbooks, timesheets, and order sheets use all four. To use them, click a cell, type if needed, and press the shortcut. A date or time is typed for you, and Enter saves it. These values are fixed. They do not change tomorrow. Each shortcut removes a small chore that would otherwise repeat hundreds of times in a busy week.

shortcut_table.action: Fill the selection with your entry

examples.scenario: A courier records today's date in a delivery logbook.
examples.why: The date is typed as a fixed value. It will not change tomorrow.

examples.scenario: A bookkeeper marks three invoices as paid at once.
examples.result: B2, B3 and B4 all show Paid
examples.why: Ctrl+Enter fills every selected cell instead of just one.

examples.scenario: A packer adds a two-line note to an order.
examples.formula: Type Rush, Alt+Enter, type Ship by Fri, Enter
examples.why: Enter would save the cell and move on. Alt+Enter keeps you inside it.

examples.scenario: A receptionist logs when a visitor arrived.
examples.result: The current time appears in B2
examples.why: The time is typed as a fixed value, not a live clock.

watch_out: Ctrl+; enters a fixed date. For a date that updates every day, use the TODAY function later in the course.
Ctrl+Enter fills the typed entry into every selected cell. Select first, then type.
recap: You can now enter common data in a single key press. Next, you will change how numbers look with number-format shortcuts.

steps.prompt: You keep a delivery logbook. In D2, enter today's date, then in E2 enter the current time, using shortcuts. Press Tab to move from D2 to E2.
hints: Two shortcuts use the semicolon key. Which one needs Shift?
Ctrl+; enters today's date and Ctrl+Shift+; enters the current time. Press Tab between them to save the date and move to the next cell.
Press Ctrl+;, then Tab, then Ctrl+Shift+;, then Enter. D2 holds today's date and E2 holds the time. On a Mac, the time is Cmd+;.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+; types today's date as a fixed value and Ctrl+Shift+; types the current time. Tab saves the date and moves to E2.

common_mistakes.message: D2 holds the time and E2 the date. The date shortcut is Ctrl+; and the time shortcut adds Shift.
Enter saved the date and moved down, so E2 is still empty. Press Tab to move to E2 first.

steps.prompt: Five invoices in E2 to E6 were all paid today. You are in E2. Mark them all Paid with a single entry.
hints: Select all five cells first. Then find the shortcut that fills every selected cell.
Shift+Down selects the cells. Type Paid, then press Ctrl+Enter (Control+Return on a Mac) to write it into every selected cell, not just the first.
Press Shift+Down four times to select E2:E6. Type Paid, then press Ctrl+Enter. All five cells show Paid.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+Enter writes your entry into every selected cell, instead of just the active one.

common_mistakes.message: Only one cell was filled. Select E2:E6 first, then press Ctrl+Enter.
You selected only four cells. Select E2:E6 with four Shift+Down presses.

steps.prompt: A delivery note in F2 needs two lines inside one cell: Rush on the first line and Ship by Fri on the second. Save the cell with Enter when you finish.
hints: Pressing Enter saves the cell. Which key combination starts a new line instead?
Alt+Enter starts a new line inside the cell and keeps you in edit mode. Enter only saves at the end (Control+Option+Return on a Mac).
Type Rush, press Alt+Enter, type Ship by Fri, then press Enter. The cell holds two lines and is saved.
steps.explanation: Alt+Enter keeps you inside the cell and starts a new line. The final Enter saves both lines together.

common_mistakes.message: Enter saved the cell after the first line. Press Alt+Enter to start a new line inside the cell.
The two lines ran together. Press Alt+Enter between them.

steps.prompt: Four new items start with a quantity of 1. You are on B2. Fill B2 to B5 with 1 in one go.
hints: The same number must go into four cells. Which keys select them and fill them together?
Select B2:B5 with Shift+Down, type the number once, then press Ctrl+Enter to write it into every selected cell (Control+Return on a Mac).
Press Shift+Down three times, type 1, then press Ctrl+Enter. B2, B3, B4 and B5 all show 1.
steps.explanation: Ctrl+Enter writes the entry into every selected cell, so one entry fills the whole block.

common_mistakes.message: Only B2 was filled. Select B2:B5 first, then press Ctrl+Enter.
You selected only three cells. Four cells need three Shift+Down presses.

steps.prompt: A customer's address needs three lines inside one cell: 12 Park Road, then Leeds, then LS1. You are in G2. Enter all three lines and save the cell.
hints: Enter saves the cell. Which key combination starts a new line inside it, twice here?
Alt+Enter starts a new line inside the cell (Control+Option+Return on a Mac). Press it between each line and save with Enter at the end.
Type 12 Park Road, press Alt+Enter, type Leeds, press Alt+Enter, type LS1, then press Enter. The cell holds three lines.
steps.explanation: Each Alt+Enter starts a new line inside the cell. The final Enter saves all three lines together.

common_mistakes.message: Enter saved the cell after the first line. Use Alt+Enter between lines.
The third line is missing. Add another Alt+Enter and LS1 before you press Enter.
The lines ran together. Press Alt+Enter between them.

title: Number Formatting Shortcuts
objectives: By the end you can change how numbers look using number-format shortcuts.
about: The same number can look very different: 1250, 1,250.00, $1,250.00, or 125000%. Number-format shortcuts change how a value is displayed without changing the value itself. Ctrl+Shift+1 adds thousands separators. Ctrl+Shift+4 shows currency. Ctrl+Shift+5 shows a percentage. Ctrl+Shift+3 shows a date. Ctrl+Shift+~ resets to General. Use them to make prices, rates, and dates readable in reports and invoices. Without them, people squint at long rows of raw numbers. To use them, select the cells and press the shortcut. Formulas still use the original number underneath, so nothing you calculate with changes. Only the way it looks changes.

examples.scenario: A shop owner formats a price as currency.
examples.why: Currency adds a symbol, thousands separators and two decimals.

examples.scenario: A manager shows a discount rate as a percentage.
examples.why: Percent multiplies the display by 100. The stored value stays 0.25.

examples.scenario: A clerk turns an exported date number into a date.
examples.why: Excel stores dates as numbers of days. The date format shows them as dates.

examples.scenario: An assistant applies percent to a whole number by mistake.
examples.why: The format only changes the display. Apply percent to 0.25, not to 25.

watch_out: The format changes how a value looks, not what it is. Formulas still use the original number.
The currency symbol follows your regional settings, so it may not be a dollar sign.
recap: You can now format numbers from the keyboard. Next, you will move between worksheets.

steps.prompt: You are in B2 on a furniture price list. Show the four prices, B2:B5, as currency.
hints: Select the four prices first. The currency shortcut uses the number key that carries the dollar sign.
Select B2:B5 with Shift+Down, then press Ctrl+Shift+4 (Control+Shift+4 on a Mac). It adds the currency symbol and two decimals.
Press Shift+Down three times, then Ctrl+Shift+4. The prices show as currency, such as $1,250.00. The values stay the same.
steps.explanation: The shortcut changes how the numbers are displayed, not the values. 1250 becomes $1,250.00 in the sheet.

common_mistakes.message: Only B2 changed. Select B2:B5 first.
That is the percent format. Currency is Ctrl+Shift+4.

steps.prompt: The discount rates in C2 to C5 are stored as decimals such as 0.15. You are in C2. Show them as percentages.
hints: The decimal 0.15 should read as a different kind of number. Which shortcut matches?
Select C2:C5, then press Ctrl+Shift+5 for percent (Control+Shift+5 on a Mac). The display is multiplied by 100 and a percent sign is added.
Press Shift+Down three times, then Ctrl+Shift+5. 0.15 shows as 15%, and the stored value stays 0.15.
steps.explanation: Percent format shows 0.15 as 15%. The stored value stays 0.15.

common_mistakes.message: That is currency. Percent is Ctrl+Shift+5.
C5 was left out. Four rates need three Shift+Down presses.

steps.prompt: E2 shows 45000, a ship date that was exported as a plain number. You are in E2. Show it as a date.
hints: A date is stored as a number of days. Which number-format shortcut turns that number into a date?
Ctrl+Shift+3 applies the date format (Control+Shift+3 on a Mac). Excel counts dates as days, so 45000 becomes a calendar date.
Press Ctrl+Shift+3. E2 shows 15-Mar-23. The cell still holds 45000, only the display changed.
steps.explanation: Excel stores dates as serial numbers. 45000 is 15 March 2023, and the date format shows it that way. The value itself does not change.

common_mistakes.message: That adds a thousands separator, so E2 would show 45,000.00. Dates use Ctrl+Shift+3.
That resets to General, which shows the plain number. Dates use Ctrl+Shift+3.

steps.prompt: City populations are hard to read as plain numbers. You are on Leeds in B2. Show B2 to B4 with thousands separators.
hints: Select all three figures first. Then find the shortcut that adds commas to big numbers.
Ctrl+Shift+1 formats numbers with thousands separators, so 1250000 reads 1,250,000.00 (Control+Shift+1 on a Mac). It changes the display, not the value.
Press Shift+Down twice to select B2:B4, then press Ctrl+Shift+1. The populations now show commas.
steps.explanation: Thousands separators make large numbers easier to read. The values themselves do not change.

common_mistakes.message: B4 was left out. Three cells need two Shift+Down presses.
That is currency. Thousands separators are Ctrl+Shift+1.

steps.prompt: E2 holds a ship date but shows $45,000.00 because currency was applied by mistake. You are in E2. Make it show a date.
hints: The cell has the wrong kind of format. Which shortcut applies the right one?
Applying a new number format replaces the old one, so you do not need to clear it first. Ctrl+Shift+3 applies the date format.
Press Ctrl+Shift+3. The currency format is replaced and E2 shows 15-Mar-23. The value 45000 never changed.
steps.explanation: A new number format replaces the old one. The date format turns 45000 into 15-Mar-23, and the value stays 45000.

common_mistakes.message: E2 still shows currency. Apply the date format with Ctrl+Shift+3.
That resets to General, which shows the plain number. Dates use Ctrl+Shift+3.

title: Worksheets
objectives: By the end you can switch, add and rename worksheets.
about: A workbook can hold many worksheets, shown as tabs along the bottom of the window. Use them to separate months, regions, or raw data from reports. Click a tab to open that sheet. Click the plus button to add a new one. Double-click a tab to rename it, so a name like Costs tells you what is inside. Shift+F11 inserts a sheet, and Ctrl+PageDown and Ctrl+PageUp move between sheets in desktop Excel. In a web browser those two keys switch browser tabs instead, so practise them in the desktop app. Here, use clicks to open, add and rename sheets.
where_to_find: Rename: double-click the sheet tab, or right-click the tab and choose Rename.
Add: click the plus button beside the tabs, or press Shift+F11 in desktop Excel.

examples.scenario: A manager keeps one sheet per month and opens March.
examples.why: Each tab is one sheet. Click it to open it.

examples.scenario: An accountant gives a default sheet a clear name.
examples.why: A clear name tells everyone what the sheet holds.

examples.scenario: A team lead adds a sheet for totals.
examples.formula: Click the plus button, then rename the new tab Summary
examples.result: A new sheet named Summary exists
examples.why: The plus button adds a sheet. Renaming it makes its purpose clear.

examples.scenario: An assistant names a sheet Costs/Income and Excel rejects it.
examples.why: Sheet names cannot contain : \ / ? * [ ]. Use Costs-Income instead.

watch_out: A new sheet is added next to the sheet you are on, so check which tab is open first.
Sheet names cannot be empty and cannot contain : \ / ? * [ ].
recap: You can now manage the sheets in a workbook. Next, Track 02 starts with formulas, where every calculation begins with an equals sign.

steps.prompt: You keep one sheet per month and are on the January sheet. Open the Mar sheet to read March's figures.
hints: Each sheet has a tab along the bottom. Which tab holds March?
The tabs along the bottom edge of the grid are the sheets. Click a tab to open that sheet. The open sheet's tab is highlighted.
Click the Mar tab at the bottom of the grid. The sheet changes to March's figures, and its tab is highlighted.
steps.explanation: Each tab is one sheet. Clicking the Mar tab opens March's sheet, which is titled March sales.

common_mistakes.message: That opened February. March is the next tab to the right.
January is still open. Click the Mar tab.

steps.prompt: A sheet holds your monthly costs but is still called Sheet2. Rename it Costs.
hints: A rename applies to the sheet you have open. Which sheet is that right now?
Open the Sheet2 tab first. Then double-click the tab, or right-click it and choose Rename, and type the new name. Press Enter to finish.
Click the Sheet2 tab, double-click it, type Costs, and press Enter. The tab now reads Costs.
steps.explanation: A rename always applies to the open sheet, so you open the tab first.

common_mistakes.message: You renamed the open sheet, Sales. Click the Sheet2 tab first, then rename.
You opened the tab but did not rename it. Double-click the tab and type the new name.

steps.prompt: Your manager wants a new sheet called Summary for the quarter's totals. Add one and name it.
hints: A new sheet is added with a button beside the tabs. It starts with a default name.
Click the plus button beside the sheet tabs to add a sheet. Then double-click its tab and type the new name. Shift+F11 also inserts a sheet.
Click the plus button, double-click the new tab, type Summary, and press Enter. The workbook now has three sheets.
steps.explanation: The plus button adds a sheet with a default name. Renaming it makes its purpose clear.

common_mistakes.message: The new sheet still needs a name. Double-click its tab and type Summary.
No sheet was added. Click the plus button beside the tabs.

steps.prompt: Two sheets are still called Sheet1 and Sheet2. Rename them January and February so the workbook is easy to read.
hints: Each rename applies to the open sheet. How will you move between the two?
Open a tab, double-click it and type the new name, then press Enter. Repeat for the second tab, because each rename affects only the open sheet.
Rename Sheet1 to January, then click Sheet2 and rename it February. Check each tab afterwards, since they show the new names.
steps.explanation: Each rename changes only the open sheet, so you open each tab in turn.

common_mistakes.message: Only one sheet was renamed. Open Sheet2 and rename it February.
You renamed Sheet1, the open sheet, to February. Open the right tab before you rename.

steps.prompt: You need a sheet for Costs/Income figures. Add one and give it a name that Excel accepts.
hints: Excel refuses some characters in sheet names. Which part of the requested name might be a problem?
Sheet names cannot contain : \ / ? * [ ]. A slash is not allowed. Replace it with a dash, a space, or an underscore, and keep both words.
Click the plus button, double-click the new tab, type Costs-Income, and press Enter. A dash replaces the slash that Excel rejects.
steps.explanation: Excel does not allow a slash in a sheet name, so a dash or a space replaces it.

common_mistakes.message: Excel does not allow a slash in a sheet name, so the name was rejected. Use a dash or a space instead.
The name must include both Costs and Income.

title: Track 01 Checkpoint: Intro to Excel
about: Three problems, one per level. Passing a level unlocks the next. Easy has hints on, Medium offers a hint only after a wrong attempt, and Hard has no hints.

steps.prompt: Your manager wants the first-quarter figures for Widget. You are in B2. Select B2:D2 using only the keyboard.
hints: You want to extend the selection sideways. Which key adds 'extend' to an arrow?
Hold Shift and press Right. Each press adds one cell to the selection. January to March is three cells, so you need two presses after the first.
Press Shift+Right twice. The selection grows from B2 to B2:D2, covering January, February and March for Widget.
steps.explanation: Shift+Right adds one cell to the selection each time. Two presses cover January to March.

common_mistakes.message: One cell short. March is in column D.
That extends downward. Use Shift+Right.

steps.prompt: You are in A1 on an order export. Select the whole table, headings included, ready to copy.
hints: You need to cover both the width and the height of the table.
Use Ctrl+Shift+Right to select to the end of the row, then Ctrl+Shift+Down to extend to the last row of the table.
Press Ctrl+Shift+Right, then Ctrl+Shift+Down. The selection becomes A1:D8, the whole table with its headings.
steps.explanation: Two jumps with Shift select the width and the height. Ctrl+A would also select the table.

common_mistakes.message: You covered the width only. Now extend downward.
You covered the height only. Now extend to the right.
Two presses of Ctrl+A selected the whole sheet. One press selects the table.

steps.prompt: A colleague pasted a stray note into this sheet. Starting from D7, select everything from A1 to the last used cell without scrolling.
steps.explanation: The last used cell is H12 because of the stray note. Ctrl+Home goes to A1, and Ctrl+Shift+End extends the selection to that corner.

common_mistakes.message: That stops at the table. The stray note in H12 makes H12 the last used cell.
You started from D7. Go to A1 first with Ctrl+Home.
Two presses of Ctrl+A select the whole sheet, which is more than the task asks.
